lesson.menu_desc: Reporting a meeting without misquoting anybody -- 33 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 9 -- What Did They Actually Say?
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Andreia Naim Finianos | Lesson 9 -- What Did They Actually Say?

listenings.text: The most expensive thing I have ever done in this job was report a meeting slightly wrong. Not a lie. Slightly wrong. The client had said they were comfortable with the timeline, and what I told my own team was that they had approved the timeline, and those are not the same sentence. Comfortable is a feeling. Approved is a decision. Six weeks later we had built to a date nobody had actually signed off, and when it came apart the client was completely right and I had nothing to stand on. What I do now is boring and it has never failed me. I write down the sentence while they are still saying it, in their words, and if I am going to repeat it to anybody I read it back to them first. It takes eleven seconds and it has saved me from that conversation about four times since.

There is a thing that happens in every second meeting and nobody names it. Somebody says, so what you are saying is, and then says something you did not say. Usually it is not malicious. They are compressing, and the compression drops the caveat. The problem is that from that moment on the room is working with their version, not yours, and if you let it go once it becomes the record. What I have learned to say, and I say it gently, is: that is close, and I would put it slightly differently. Then I say my version. Nobody has ever taken offence. And the reverse is just as important. When I am the one summarising somebody else, I say, tell me if I have got this wrong, and about a third of the time they do tell me, and that third is where the whole deal lives.
